properties.description: cargo-semver-checks runs in CI across the workspace against the most recent release tag, DERIVED at run time via `git describe --tags --abbrev=0` rather than a hand-maintained literal, and the job fails loudly if no tag exists instead of treating an absent baseline as a pass. It matters more here than in a published crate: consumers pin by git tag and link these crates directly, so an unnoticed breaking change lands in their build rather than in a registry's version resolution. It is also the only check that can catch a Cargo FEATURE rename, which is a downstream build break that no public-API diff, OpenAPI document or published surface would mention (req:feature-names-are-contract). The baseline was a literal `v0.4.0` until 2026-07-28 while the workspace was at 0.11.0 — seven minors of drift, during which Cargo's 0.x rules made the comparison permit every breaking change it was meant to catch.

dynograph-client
properties.purpose: Async reqwest client for /v1, over TCP or a same-host Unix socket. One method per route, transport-agnostic.

properties.name: dynograph-cluster
properties.purpose: Density-based clustering (DBSCAN) over a PRECOMPUTED distance matrix. Matrix in, labels out — it deliberately does not compute distances, the same way it does not produce vectors.

properties.name: dynograph-core
properties.purpose: The schema model that drives the entire engine: Schema, NodeTypeDef, EdgeTypeDef, Value, DynoError, and YAML/JSON parse plus validation. A schema is a RUNTIME description of what nodes and edges may exist — which is what lets one binary serve any domain.

properties.name: Schema-driven engine
properties.purpose: The graph engine proper: the schema model everything is driven by, the storage engine that validates and indexes against it, the derived full-text view, and entity resolution.

properties.name: dynograph-game
properties.purpose: Closed-form normal-form game-theory analysis: dominant strategies, pure-strategy Nash equilibria, Pareto optimality, and the prisoner's-dilemma classification.

properties.name: dynograph-graph
properties.purpose: Domain-neutral graph-theory algorithms over a densely-indexed in-memory graph: centrality, components, communities, paths and flow. Every algorithm is EXACT — no approximate or streaming variants — because consumer graphs are small.

properties.name: Pure primitives
properties.purpose: Dependency-free math crates: no storage, no service, no dependency even on dynograph-core. Matrix/vectors/graphs in, results out. This is the layer that makes the workspace reusable outside its own service.

properties.name: dynograph-resolution
properties.purpose: Three-tier entity resolution — auto-merge above the high threshold, vector tiebreaker in the middle band, new entity below the low one — with a source-aware path that reserves auto-merge for name-to-name evidence.

properties.name: dynograph-service
properties.purpose: The axum HTTP service and the `dynograph` binary: a multi-graph registry, pluggable auth, the /v1 REST surface, operational probes, Prometheus metrics, and a generated OpenAPI contract. By far the largest crate in the workspace.

properties.name: dynograph-storage
properties.purpose: Schema-validated node and edge persistence: column families for nodes, edges, adjacency and the reverse index; MessagePack values; graph isolation so many graphs share one instance; atomic batch writes; iterator scans; a read cache; and the optional full-text mirror.

properties.name: Network surface
properties.purpose: The HTTP service that hosts many independent graphs over the engine, and the async client for it.

properties.name: dynograph-text
properties.purpose: Tantivy-backed BM25 keyword index behind a small storage-agnostic API. Knows nothing about schemas or graphs: callers pass already-extracted (graph, node_type, node_id, fields) and get scored node ids back.

properties.name: dynograph-vector
properties.purpose: f32/f64 vector and statistics math plus the HNSW approximate-nearest-neighbour index: SIMD cosine similarity, the distance family, element-wise algebra, transforms, and descriptive statistics through to correlation.

properties.name: Consumer graphs are 10^2-10^3 nodes
properties.statement: The stated scale assumption behind choosing exact algorithms over approximate or streaming ones. Worth surfacing because it is the assumption that would have to be revisited first if a consumer graph grew by orders of magnitude — and reflow2's own design graph is already ~790 nodes.

properties.name: Container image ~80 MB
properties.statement: The canonical target for the published image; strip=debuginfo exists to reach it from 99.8 MB while keeping symbols for backtraces.

properties.name: MSRV 1.94
properties.statement: The workspace requires Rust 1.94 or newer, because is_multiple_of (used in the storage engine's embedding decode) stabilized there. Pinned in lockstep with the Dockerfile toolchain so a local build fails with a clear MSRV error rather than a missing-method error.

properties.decision: Every algorithm in dynograph-graph is exact; no approximate or streaming variants are offered.
properties.name: Choose exact algorithms over approximate ones
properties.rationale: Consumer graphs are small — 10^2 to 10^3 nodes — so the usual reason to approximate does not apply, and an exact answer removes a whole class of 'is this real or is this the approximation?' questions from the consumer's side.

properties.decision: Treat `rocksdb` and `fulltext` as named, stable parts of the dynograph-storage contract. Renaming or removing either is a breaking change requiring the same care as a signature change. RATIFIED by Anthony 2026-07-28; the earlier answer given to reflow2 — that the names were an internal they relied on at their own risk — no longer stands and has been superseded in the coordination channel.
properties.name: Commit to the feature names rather than leave a consumer exposed
properties.rationale: Cargo features are public API in practice: a downstream crate forwards to them by name in its own manifest, so a rename is a downstream build break with no compile-time warning on either side. The design already commits to the CAPABILITIES being feature-gated — RocksDB ships default-on behind a switch, the full-text index is a derived view — and committing to the switch names costs almost nothing while removing a real, currently-silent exposure. The alternative, keeping the freedom to rename, is defensible but should then be stated to consumers rather than left undiscussed, which is how it stood until the seam exercise surfaced it.

properties.decision: The Tantivy index is a derived, rebuildable view; the caller's primary store is the source of truth. Writes are buffered against Tantivy's own commit lifecycle.
properties.name: Make the full-text index derived rather than transactional
properties.rationale: Tantivy cannot join RocksDB's atomic write batch, so a transactional guarantee across both is not available at any price. Rather than pretend, the design names the index as derived and rebuildable — which makes an inconsistency a rebuild rather than a corruption.

properties.decision: The spec is generated from handlers and wire types, served at /openapi.json, and the generated document is committed and checked in CI.
properties.name: Generate the OpenAPI contract from the code, and commit the result
properties.rationale: A hand-maintained spec drifts from the code silently, and consumers generate their clients from it. Generating it makes drift impossible in one direction; committing it and failing CI on a difference makes an unreviewed contract change impossible in the other.

properties.decision: Community detection uses the deterministic greedy Leiden variant; the request and response contract is unchanged.
properties.name: Replace Louvain with Leiden for community detection
properties.rationale: Leiden's refinement phase repairs Louvain's one real defect — communities that come out badly connected or even internally disconnected — so every returned community is now guaranteed internally connected. The deterministic variant was chosen to preserve the suite's reproducibility invariant, so the guarantee comes from the refinement structure rather than from randomness.

properties.decision: The KvBackend trait stays at the raw-KV level: column families addressed by name, opaque byte keys and values, and ordered prefix iteration as the one structural assumption.
properties.name: Put the backend seam at raw bytes, not at the graph level
properties.rationale: Keeping the seam narrow is what makes 'implement one trait' a true claim. Everything schema-aware — validation, the reverse index, the read cache, the write-buffer overlay, the full-text sidecar — stays above it, so a new backend inherits all of that rather than reimplementing it. The cost is that every backend must honour ordered prefix iteration, because adjacency and index scans are built on it.

properties.decision: publish=false at the workspace level; the documented consumption form is a git tag.
properties.name: Do not publish to crates.io; consume by git tag
properties.rationale: Stated in the manifest as a considered position, not an oversight: it makes cargo-deny's allow-wildcard-paths apply to internal path deps and prevents an accidental publish of a crate not yet audited for crates.io readiness (internal deps carry no explicit versions). The comment records exactly what flipping it would require.

properties.decision: As of v0.11.0 TextIndex::search matches tokens as a ranked disjunction: a document needs at least one token, and results come back in descending BM25 order. Previously every token had to occur.
properties.name: Rank a multi-term query instead of excluding on it
properties.rationale: The conjunctive form made a natural-language question unusable — one incidental word the corpus never used collapsed a perfect match to zero results. And zero hits reads as 'no such thing exists' to a caller who searches before creating a node, so the false negative manufactured duplicates: the index was degrading the graph it exists to protect. The conjunctive test was FLIPPED rather than deleted, so the contract change is on the record.

properties.decision: The rocksdb cargo feature is enabled by default, so the shipped binary and library behave as they always have; --no-default-features drops it.
properties.name: Ship RocksDB on by default, behind a feature that can be turned off
properties.rationale: Two audiences with opposite needs: production wants durable storage without thinking about it, while CI and consumers who do not need persistence want to skip a ~10-minute C++ compile. Default-on keeps the common path unchanged and makes the fast path opt-in.

properties.decision:
Reach RocksDB C++ 11.8.1 by bumping the existing `rocksdb` dependency 0.24 -> 0.25, rather than by switching to the `rust-rocksdb` crate.

STATUS 2026-08-24: committed on branch chore/rocksdb-0.25 at b4d31eb. The gating on-disk rollback probe PASSED — see frag:idea-rocksdb-ondisk-format for the method and its limits. Cold-build cost measured at +51% (fact:rocksdb-cold-build-baseline-2026-08-24). Not yet pushed, reviewed, or released.

WHY THE FORK LOST. The upgrade was first framed as "update from rocksdb to rust-rocksdb, which is at v0.52.0", on the understanding that 0.24 -> 0.52 was a version gap. It is not. They are two crates:
  `rocksdb`      github.com/rust-rocksdb/rust-rocksdb (the org). Published since 2014-11-29. 52.8M downloads total, 6.4M recent.
  `rust-rocksdb` github.com/zaidoon1/rust-rocksdb — a fork by one individual, first published 2024-02-10. 804K total, 550K recent. No maintainers named besides the owner.
So adopting it would have been a fork adoption — new maintainer, single-person bus factor, its own advisory surface to track under deny.toml — and not the version bump it looked like.

WHAT DECIDED IT. Mainline `rocksdb` 0.25.0 was released 2026-08-16, eight days before this session, and depends on librocksdb-sys 0.19.0+11.8.1 — the exact C++ engine version wanted from the fork. The engine was reachable without leaving the crate we already use, for a one-line change.

WHAT THE FORK STILL HAS, so this can be revisited honestly: a much faster release cadence against a slow upstream (mainline went 0.23 Dec-2024 -> 0.24 Aug-2025 -> 0.25 Aug-2026). If mainline stalls again, that argument returns. It was simply at its weakest possible moment here.

CORRECTION WORTH KEEPING: the fork's README states a rolling 6-month MSRV policy at 1.91.0, not the 1.88.0 in the notes this was argued from — so that source was imprecise, which matters when it is the basis for a decision.

TWO OF THE FOUR ADVERTISED BENEFITS DO NOT REACH THIS PROJECT AT ALL, checked against the repo rather than assumed: the MSRV floor is moot (workspace already at rust-version 1.94, toolchain 1.95.0), and the jemalloc 0.7 change is invisible (jemalloc appears zero times in Cargo.lock). AIX is irrelevant to a Linux x86_64 container. Only the engine bump had substance.

WHAT WAS NEVER MEASURED, and should not be claimed: whether 11.8.1's LSM-tree work actually helps this project. No performance baseline exists and no consumer's real on-disk store size is known (frag:idea-rocksdb-real-data-scale). The honest case for this bump is currency, not speed.
properties.name: Take RocksDB 11.8.1 from mainline `rocksdb` 0.25, not the zaidoon1 fork
properties.rationale: The engine version wanted was available on the incumbent crate; adopting a single-maintainer fork to get the same thing would have added supply-chain surface for no gain. The gating on-disk rollback probe subsequently PASSED (2026-08-24), and the cold-build cost was measured at +51%.

properties.decision: resolve_sourced is the recommended entry point: auto-merge is reserved for name-to-name evidence, alias-sourced matches always require vector corroboration, and an incoming alias matching two or more candidates is excluded.
properties.name: Let the SOURCE of a match decide what the match may do
properties.rationale: An alias is weaker evidence than a name, and treating them alike let a nickname collapse two real entities. Making the evidence source part of the rule keeps the strong action (auto-merge) tied to the strong evidence.

properties.decision:
OPEN — raised 2026-08-24 during the RocksDB 10.4.2 -> 11.8.1 bump, not settled. Recorded so the next engine bump does not re-derive it.

THE PROBLEM. The Rust API does not move across this bump, so semver says patch. But the on-disk engine underneath changes, and req:consume-by-tag says consumers pin these crates BY GIT TAG and hold live on-disk stores. 'Your storage engine changed' is arguably not a patch-level fact even when every type signature is identical.

THE PART THAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN A NAMING QUESTION, found while looking: this project already HAS a guard for exactly this worry — cap:semver-guard / ver:semver, running `cargo semver-checks --workspace against a baseline revision`, existing to satisfy req:no-silent-breaking-change. IT STRUCTURALLY CANNOT SEE THIS CLASS OF CHANGE. semver-checks reads the public API surface; an engine swap underneath an unchanged surface is invisible to it. So the guard would pass, green, on a change that alters what happens to consumers' data.

WHAT IS NOT AT STAKE: this particular bump was probed and rolls back (frag:idea-rocksdb-ondisk-format), so it is not a one-way door. The question is about the CLASS, not this instance — a future engine bump that IS one-way would clear the same green guard.

OPTIONS NOT YET WEIGHED: treat storage-engine version as part of the published contract the way req:feature-names-are-contract treats feature names; or add a separate check that fails when librocksdb-sys's bundled version moves; or decide the tag+CHANGELOG is enough and this is a documentation duty, not a gate.
properties.name: How to classify a release whose API is unchanged but whose storage engine is not

properties.decision: StorageEngine::search_fulltext returns dynograph_storage::FulltextHit rather than dynograph_text::TextHit. The new type carries the same three fields, converts From<TextHit> inside the storage crate, and is #[non_exhaustive] so a later field is not a breaking change. TextError also becomes #[non_exhaustive].
properties.name: Give the storage boundary its own full-text hit type
properties.rationale: Found by the seam exercise with a consumer project: it consumes search_fulltext and reads all three fields, so a change to a dynograph-text type would break a consumer that never names dynograph-text and could not have learned the coupling from the published surface. Owning the type at the boundary that publishes it makes the dependency honest. Chosen over re-exporting TextHit, which would have stabilised the path without removing the coupling. Breaking in the semver sense but source-compatible for every known consumer: both call sites in this workspace, and that consumer's, read fields rather than naming the type; the other known consumer has no Rust use of this surface at all.

properties.name: Strip debuginfo but keep symbols in release builds
properties.rationale: Keeps function names in backtraces while dropping 20-30 MB, bringing the image toward the ~80 MB target. Debug builds are untouched, so RUST_BACKTRACE on a debug build still gives line numbers.

properties.rationale: TRUE, and it is the architecture rather than a fault. dynograph-service is the only crate that depends on the pure-primitive layer (vector, graph, game, cluster), so every path from those to the rest of the workspace goes through it — which is exactly what 'pure, dependency-free primitives' means. The usual remedy for a single point of failure, adding redundancy, is meaningless here: nothing is failing over, and a second path would mean a second consumer of the primitives, which is a reason to build one, not a repair. Worth revisiting only if a primitive crate needs to reach storage or core directly — at which point the layering, not the SPOF, is the thing that changed.

properties.summary:
QUESTION SETTLED 2026-08-24 by direct lookup on crates.io. They are NOT the same crate and 0.24-vs-0.52 was never a version gap — it is two separate lineages.

`rocksdb` (what we depend on today)
  repo: github.com/rust-rocksdb/rust-rocksdb (the ORG — mainline)
  first published 2014-11-29; latest 0.25.0 on 2026-08-16
  52,796,551 total downloads / 6,368,386 recent

`rust-rocksdb` (the crate the user proposed)
  repo: github.com/zaidoon1/rust-rocksdb — a FORK maintained by one named individual
  first published 2024-02-10; latest 0.52.0 on 2026-08-08
  804,046 total downloads / 549,532 recent
  README rationale: regular RocksDB updates, rolling 6-month MSRV policy (states 1.91.0, NOT the 1.88.0 in the user's notes), active maintenance, quick issue resolution. No maintainers named besides the owner.

CONSEQUENCE: adopting it is a fork adoption — new maintainer, single-person bus factor, own advisory tracking under deny.toml — exactly as the counter-argument anticipated. It is NOT a version bump.

BUT SEE frag:idea-rocksdb-mainline-025 — the fork is no longer the only route to the engine the user wanted.
properties.title: SETTLED: `rocksdb` and `rust-rocksdb` are two different crates

properties.intent: Recorded as an idea under consideration. The only one of the user's four listed items with real substance.
properties.summary:
User: "Underlying C++ engine upgrade v10.4.2 -> v11.8.1. This brings critical upstream LSM-tree optimizations, multi-row transactional logic changes, and internal memory architecture updates. Can we take advantage of any of these?"

CONFIRMED CURRENT STATE: Cargo.lock has librocksdb-sys 0.17.3+10.4.2, so the 10.4.2 figure checks out.

UPDATE 2026-08-24: 11.8.1 is reachable via mainline `rocksdb` 0.25.0 — no fork adoption needed. See frag:idea-rocksdb-mainline-025.

COUNTER: we cannot observe the benefit. No RocksDB performance baseline exists, and the prior advanced-features assessment already concluded measure-first.

BUILD-TIME COUNTER, CORRECTED after the user pushed back: the user is right that build.rs caches the compiled C++ engine in target/ and emits rerun-if-changed, so editing Rust code does not rebuild it and the warm edit-test loop stays fast. VERIFIED, and verified to be ALREADY TRUE: our current librocksdb-sys 0.17.3+10.4.2 ships that same build.rs (2 rerun-if-changed directives), and the Dockerfile already uses BuildKit cache mounts for /build/target and the cargo registry. So this is the status quo, not a v0.52 gain.

The build-time cost therefore narrows to COLD builds, which caching does not touch: fresh CI runs, the published image build, fresh clones, and any Cargo.toml/feature-flag change that invalidates the cache. A larger C++ engine makes those longer, and the image build lands on req:image-size.

DEPENDS ON: frag:idea-rocksdb-ondisk-format (the real risk, unchanged) and frag:idea-rocksdb-real-data-scale (may make this moot).
properties.title: IDEA: take the C++ engine from RocksDB 10.4.2 to 11.8.1

GCC 15 HALF: possibly real. Every storage-touching build on this machine currently needs BINDGEN_EXTRA_CLANG_ARGS="-isystem /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/15/include" because clang is absent and bindgen cannot find stdbool.h. If native GCC 15 support deletes that workaround it is a small but genuine papercut removal on a command run constantly.

COST: cheap to test, once the crate-identity question is settled.

properties.intent: A third option that did not exist when the brainstorm was recorded. Found while settling the crate-identity question.
properties.summary:
Mainline `rocksdb` released 0.25.0 on 2026-08-16 — EIGHT DAYS before this brainstorm — and it depends on librocksdb-sys 0.19.0+11.8.1.

That is RocksDB C++ 11.8.1: the exact engine version the user wanted from the fork.

librocksdb-sys lineage, verbatim from crates.io:
  0.19.0+11.8.1  2026-08-16   <- available on mainline now
  0.17.3+10.4.2  2025-08-10   <- what we are pinned to
  0.17.1+9.9.3   2024-12-24

SO THE HEADLINE ITEM IS REACHABLE WITHOUT ADOPTING A FORK: `rocksdb = "0.24"` -> `"0.25"` is a one-line change on the crate we already use, from the org that has maintained it since 2014, with 6.4M recent downloads behind it.

What this does NOT settle: the on-disk format and rollback question (frag:idea-rocksdb-ondisk-format) is unchanged — 11.8.1 is 11.8.1 whichever crate delivers it, so the migration risk is identical and still must be answered first.

What it DOES weaken: the fork's main selling point is release cadence against a slow upstream (mainline went 0.23 Dec-2024 -> 0.24 Aug-2025 -> 0.25 Aug-2026). With 0.25.0 just out and current on the engine, that argument is at its weakest point in two years.
properties.title: FINDING: mainline `rocksdb` 0.25.0 already ships RocksDB 11.8.1

properties.intent: The user's follow-up question: "there were a lot of unknowns in your statement - how can we measure to determine if an upgrade is valuable?"
properties.summary:
OBSERVATION FROM THE GRAPH: of 23 Requirements in this design, NOT ONE states a latency or throughput target. So "is it faster" currently has no pass/fail line to be judged against — which is why the engine-bump case could not be argued either way.

The two budgets that DO exist are req:image-size (the published image should stay near the ~80 MB target) and req:msrv-locked-to-image. Both are measurable today and both could be VIOLATED by a bigger C++ engine. So the design's existing budgets CONSTRAIN this upgrade even though none of them REWARD it.

OPEN: do we want a stated performance budget at all, or is absence-of-regression the honest bar for a dependency bump? Recorded as an idea, not as a requirement.
properties.title: IDEA: what yardstick would tell us a RocksDB upgrade was valuable?

BUT NOT A FREE VARIABLE: req:msrv-locked-to-image says the MSRV must be pinned in lockstep with the container toolchain. So even though the floor is already satisfied, MSRV is governed and cannot drift casually.

properties.intent: Not in the user's list. Raised during brainstorm as the real risk hiding inside the engine bump.
properties.summary:
PROBED 2026-08-24 with crates/dynograph-storage/examples/rocksdb_roundtrip, a scratch harness run from two checkouts differing only in the rocksdb crate version.

RESULT — the full cycle passed:
  1. 10.4.2 created the store and wrote a marker.
  2. 11.8.1 opened it, READ the 10.4.2 marker, and wrote its own.
  3. 10.4.2 REOPENED it and read BOTH markers.

So the upgrade is not one-way. A consumer pinning by git tag (req:consume-by-tag) can move to 11.8.1 and back again against the same on-disk store.

VERIFIED BEFORE BELIEVING IT: the 0.24 rebuild finished in 0.65 s because cargo reused cached artifacts, which would have made the rollback leg meaningless if it had actually reused the 11.8.1 binary. Checked — the two binaries differ in hash and size (225,937,432 vs 256,184,864 bytes) and embed different engine version strings (10.4.2 vs 11.8.1). The test is valid.

LIMITS, so this is not read as more than it is: a small store, default options, no compaction pressure, a single schema, one column-family layout. It shows the format is not GRATUITOUSLY one-way. It does not prove rollback safety for a large production store under compaction, nor for every option combination — new table formats are typically opt-in, so a future option change could still create a one-way door.
properties.title: ANSWERED: on-disk format survives 10.4.2 -> 11.8.1, and rolls back

properties.intent: Not in the user's list. Raised during brainstorm as the cheapest question that could make the expensive ones moot.
properties.summary:
MEASURED 2026-08-24 by sweeping the development workstation where the consumer projects live.

Every RocksDB store found belonging to a consumer of these crates: ONE, at 152 KB.

(Several larger RocksDB stores exist on that machine — 244 KB to 89 MB — but they belong to a different product's design graphs, not to consumers of dynograph.)

A FALSE LEAD WORTH RECORDING so it is not re-followed: `du` first showed three data directories at 84 MB, 3.0 MB and 28 KB, which looked like substantial consumer stores. None are RocksDB — no CURRENT file, and their contents are JSON corpora and a SQLite database. None of those projects has a dynograph dependency in its Cargo.toml. The 84 MB figure meant nothing.

CONSEQUENCE, and it closes the performance half of the engine question: at 152 KB the data does not fill one memtable. There is no level structure and no compaction pressure, so RocksDB 11.8.1's LSM-tree optimizations CANNOT produce a measurable difference here. No benchmark would show anything, which means the benchmark harness contemplated in this brainstorm — the largest single piece of work proposed — should NOT be built. There is nothing for it to measure.

So the +51% cold-build cost buys zero performance for any consumer that exists today, and the honest case for the bump is currency alone. That was already the stated position; it is now measured rather than suspected.

LIMIT: one machine was swept. Consumers running elsewhere — a deployed container, another workstation, a machine not reachable from here — were not measured and could hold larger stores. This is evidence about the development estate, not proof about every deployment.
properties.title: ANSWERED: the largest real consumer store is 152 KB — LSM gains are unobservable

properties.title: Cargo.toml

properties.name: AuthProvider trait
properties.spec: The pluggable authentication seam for the service. Shipped providers are `noauth` (the default) and `bearer_jwt`. An EXTENSION POINT.

properties.name: DynographClient API
properties.spec: One async method per /v1 route, returning the corresponding wire type. Transport is chosen at construction (TCP base URL or Unix socket path) and the methods are identical either way.

properties.name: DBSCAN clustering API
properties.spec: Precomputed N-by-N distance matrix in, per-point cluster label or noise out.

properties.name: Core model types (Schema, Value, DynoError)
properties.spec: The vocabulary every other crate and every consumer speaks: the schema types, the dynamic Value, and the error enum. Changing an error variant or a Value case is a breaking change for every consumer, which is why cargo-semver-checks runs in CI.

properties.name: Game-theory analysis API
properties.spec: Game::from_cells then analyze; returns dominant strategies, pure Nash equilibria, Pareto-optimal outcomes and the nash_is_pareto_suboptimal classification.

properties.name: Graph algorithms API
properties.operations: centrality, connected components, community detection (Leiden), shortest paths, max flow
properties.spec: Caller builds a Graph via GraphBuilder — interning string ids, supplying finite f64 weights and a directed flag — and results come back keyed by dense node index for the caller to map back. No storage, service or core dependency.

properties.name: KvBackend trait (storage seam)
properties.operations: six byte-level primitives over six named column families, plus ordered prefix iteration
properties.spec: The narrow seam underneath StorageEngine. All schema-aware behaviour — validation, the reverse index, the read cache, the write-buffer overlay, the full-text sidecar — sits ABOVE this trait; everything that touches bytes goes through it. Ordered prefix iteration is the one structural assumption every backend must honour, because the adjacency and index scans are built on it. An EXTENSION POINT: implementing it is how a new backend (Postgres, sled) arrives without the engine changing.

properties.name: Operational probes and metrics
properties.spec: Public and unauthenticated by design, because an orchestrator's liveness check and a Prometheus scrape cannot hold a credential. /ready is deliberately distinct from /health. /metrics is Prometheus text format; /buildinfo carries version and git SHA.

properties.name: EntityResolver API
properties.payload_schema: Types crossing this boundary: Candidate, EntityResolver, MatchSource, ResolutionOutcome, ResolutionResult (owned here), plus HnswIndex and HnswConfig (dynograph-vector) and ResolutionConfig / ResolutionStrategy (dynograph-core), all RE-EXPORTED from this crate so a caller can name them without depending on the source crates directly. HnswIndex is a PARAMETER of resolve / resolve_with_aliases / resolve_sourced, so a caller must construct one — the strongest form of cross-boundary coupling here. See req:boundaries-own-their-types.
properties.spec: resolve / resolve_sourced. The source-aware path is the recommended entry point: auto-merge is reserved for name-to-name evidence, alias-sourced matches always require vector corroboration, and an incoming alias matching two or more candidates is excluded rather than guessed at.

properties.error_model: JSON error body; 501 for routes whose build feature is off — the route and its OpenAPI entry always exist, so the contract does not change with the feature set
properties.name: /v1 REST API
properties.operations: 80 operations across graph lifecycle, schema, nodes, edges, embeddings, search, primitives, algo/* and util/*
properties.spec: The complete published HTTP surface. Auth is a bearer JWT when configured for it; the default configuration is `noauth`. TLS is not terminated by the service itself.

properties.error_model: DynoError::Validation naming the node type and property
properties.name: Schema document (YAML/JSON)
properties.operations: parse, validate; POST /v1/graphs to configure a graph
properties.payload_schema: dynograph_core::Schema — node_types, edge_types, property flags (type/required/range/enum/default, indexed, fulltext), embedding_field, resolution rules
properties.spec: THE central contract of the whole workspace. Each declaration is what TURNS ON a capability: `indexed` enables scans and where-prefilters, `fulltext` enables keyword search, `embedding_field` enables vector similarity, `resolution` enables dedup. The engine has no hardcoded domain types — only the ones a schema names.

properties.name: StorageEngine Rust API
properties.operations: create/read/update/delete nodes and edges, adjacency and index scans, atomic batches, embedding sidecar operations, full-text mirroring
properties.payload_schema: Types crossing this boundary are owned by dynograph-storage: Schema and Value from dynograph-core (the shared vocabulary), StoredNode, StoredEdge, CacheConfig, and FulltextHit. `search_fulltext` returns FulltextHit, NOT dynograph_text::TextHit — see dec:storage-owns-its-hit-type. The `rocksdb` and `fulltext` Cargo feature names are part of this contract because consumers forward to them by name (dec:feature-names-committed, awaiting ratification).
properties.spec: The embedded-library entry point: `StorageEngine::new_in_memory(schema)` or a RocksDB path, then typed CRUD validated against the schema. This is the contract consumer projects are built on, so its stability matters more than its elegance.

properties.name: TextIndex API
properties.spec: Index a node's full-text fields, remove it, and run tokenized BM25 keyword search. Storage-agnostic: callers pass (graph, node_type, node_id, fields) and get scored node ids back. Since v0.11.0 a multi-term query is a RANKED DISJUNCTION rather than a conjunction — a document must contain at least one token, and results come back in descending BM25 order.

properties.name: Same-host Unix-socket transport
properties.spec: The identical JSON /v1 API over a Unix domain socket, for faster same-host calls. Access to the socket file IS the network boundary, which is why transport security is filesystem permission rather than TLS.

properties.name: Vector, HNSW and statistics API
properties.spec: HNSW index plus the distance family, element-wise algebra, transforms and descriptive statistics through to Pearson and Spearman correlation.

properties.description: Rust workspace of domain-agnostic foundation crates for graph-based projects: schema-driven graph storage on RocksDB, HNSW vector search, BM25 full-text, entity resolution, pure graph/game/cluster math, and an HTTP service over all of it. Usable as embedded library crates or as the `dynograph` binary. Deliberately domain-neutral — extractors, schemas and servers for a domain live in CONSUMER projects and depend on these crates by git tag.
properties.name: dynograph-foundation

properties.context_setter: Nothing asked for capability “Be operable: probes, metrics and build identity”
properties.question: Distinct /health and /ready probes, Prometheus metrics, and a /buildinfo with the git SHA — everything a serious deployment needs, and nothing states it as a requirement. Is there an operating standard behind it (a Kubernetes deployment, a scrape config) that should be recorded, or was it built to the obvious shape?

properties.context_setter: Nothing asked for capability “Choose how callers prove who they are”
properties.question: Auth is pluggable (noauth and bearer-JWT shipped, a trait for more), and the default is noauth. Was pluggability the goal, or is it the shape that fell out of needing one real provider? It matters because a published extension point is a commitment.

properties.context_setter: Nothing asked for capability “Atomic batch writes”
properties.question: Batch writes are described in the crate as being 'for extraction integration' — which reads like a specific consumer's need. Whose? If a consumer depends on all-or-nothing writes, that is a stated guarantee rather than an optimisation, and worth recording as one.

properties.context_setter: Nothing asked for capability “Change a live graph's schema”
properties.question: There is a schema-evolution path so a configured graph is not frozen at creation — but unlike every other capability here, it appears in no document at all, not even the endpoint catalogue's own framing. Is changing a live graph's schema a supported promise, or something that works and nobody wants to advertise yet?

properties.context_setter: Nothing asked for capability “Classify a normal-form game”
properties.question: dynograph-game ships full normal-form game-theory analysis — dominant strategies, Nash equilibria, Pareto optimality — and the service exposes it. No document in the repo says what it is for. Is there a consumer using it, is it groundwork for one, or is it something that landed and stayed?

properties.context_setter: Nothing asked for capability “Cluster points by density from a distance matrix”
properties.question: dynograph-cluster does DBSCAN over a precomputed distance matrix, and its own doc is careful that it is NOT a graph algorithm. Same question: which consumer asked for density clustering, and is it earning its place in a graph foundation?

properties.context_setter: Nothing satisfies requirement “A published boundary must not leak a type owned by another boundary”
properties.question: Each part of this project hands out its own kinds of data at its edges. We just found a case where the storage part was handing out a piece of data that really belonged to the search part — so anyone using storage could be broken by a change to search, without ever knowing the two were connected. That case is now fixed and the rule is written down, but nothing actually checks the rule. If the same mistake were made elsewhere tomorrow, no test would catch it and it would surface only when someone else's build broke. Do you want a check built to enforce this across every boundary, is fixing the one known case enough for now, or would you rather this stay guidance for people rather than something automated?

properties.answer: "ratify both decisions and fix the semver baseline" — Anthony chose the first of the three options offered: make the promise real AND make it enforced. Recorded as dec:feature-names-committed (accepted) and req:feature-names-are-contract (accepted). The enforcement half was implemented by DERIVING the semver baseline from the most recent release tag rather than bumping the hand-maintained literal, because a hand-maintained baseline is the step that had already failed for seven minors. reflow2 has been told to flip their agreement row from "declared and refused" to "declared and committed".
properties.context_setter: Nothing satisfies requirement “Cargo feature names are part of the published contract”
properties.question: You've now written down a promise that the build switches named `rocksdb` and `fulltext` will keep those names, because reflow2's build refers to them by name and would break instantly if they changed. But nothing currently checks that promise — if someone renamed one tomorrow, no test or CI job would notice. The check that could enforce it is the semver guard, and it is comparing against a baseline seven releases out of date, so it is not really looking. Do you want the semver baseline fixed so this promise is actually enforced, do you want to keep the promise as an honest statement of intent that nothing verifies for now, or would you rather not make the promise at all and tell reflow2 they rename at their own risk?

properties.description: Ranked-disjunction full-text search. The release reflow2 depends on by tag.
properties.name: v0.11.0
Graph algorithms must be exact, not approximate
properties.statement: dynograph-graph's own doc: consumer graphs are small (10^2-10^3 nodes), so every algorithm is exact — no approximate or streaming variants. A scale assumption stated as a design rule.

properties.name: An alias-sourced match must not auto-merge on name similarity alone
properties.statement: The resolution crate doc, from v0.9.3: auto-merge is reserved for name-to-name evidence, alias-sourced matches always require vector corroboration, and an incoming alias matching two or more candidates is excluded rather than resolved. A rule about which EVIDENCE justifies which action.

properties.name: Changing the storage backend must not change the engine
properties.statement: README: all schema-aware logic sits above a narrow KvBackend trait, and moving to PostgreSQL, SQLite or sled is 'a matter of implementing that one trait; nothing in the graph engine has to change.'

properties.name: Every type crossing a published boundary must be nameable through that boundary
properties.statement:
A consumer must be able to name every type in a signature it has to satisfy, using only the crate that publishes the signature. Two remedies, chosen by whether the source crate is optional:

(1) REQUIRED dependency -> RE-EXPORT. The type is always present and is usually shared vocabulary (Schema, Value, DynoError from dynograph-core; HnswIndex from dynograph-vector). Wrapping would fork the vocabulary for no gain. Without the re-export a consumer must add the source crate to its own manifest at a version nobody stated, which is an undeclared coupling and a version-sync hazard.

(2) OPTIONAL dependency -> OWN THE TYPE. A consumer cannot depend on a crate that may not be compiled into the build, so re-export is not enough; the publishing crate must define its own type and convert. This is the sharper case because the coupling is invisible from both sides.

Worked cases, all found by the 2026-07-28 seam exercise with reflow2. Optional: StorageEngine::search_fulltext returned dynograph_text::TextHit, reached only through the `fulltext` feature — now dynograph_storage::FulltextHit. Required: EntityResolver's resolve* methods take Option<&HnswIndex> as a PARAMETER (worse than a return type, since the caller must construct one); StoredNode/StoredEdge properties are HashMap<String, Value> and every storage method returns DynoError; GraphRegistry::create_graph takes Schema and hnsw_stats_snapshot returns HnswStats — all now re-exported.

properties.name: Every returned community must be internally connected
properties.statement: CHANGELOG v0.10.0: Leiden replaced Louvain specifically because Louvain could return communities that were badly connected or internally disconnected; the guarantee comes from the refinement structure.

properties.name: Consumers depend on these crates by git tag, not crates.io
properties.statement: README and the manifest: nothing is published to crates.io, publish=false is set at the workspace level, and the documented dependency form is a git tag. The manifest comment records what publishing would require, so this is a considered position rather than an oversight.

properties.name: The published API contract must not be able to drift from the code
properties.statement: README: the OpenAPI document is generated from the handlers and wire types 'so it can't drift from the running code', and a CI test fails if the code changes the contract without the committed spec being regenerated.

properties.name: Algorithm results must be reproducible run to run
properties.statement: CHANGELOG v0.10.0: the deterministic greedy Leiden variant was chosen over the randomized one to preserve the suite's reproducibility invariant.

properties.name: Published facts in the docs must match the code, and the check must not be able to go quiet
properties.statement: scripts/check-doc-versions.sh, run in CI, catches the class of drift where a release bump lands in Cargo.toml while the docs still advertise the previous tag, and where a documented route count no longer matches the published contract (counted from docs/openapi.json, which a contract-gate test pins to the generated spec). Because each check is anchored on a literal doc phrase, a reworded doc would otherwise disable it silently, so a pattern that matches nothing anywhere fails the run: a check that has stopped looking must not be able to report the same clean result as a check that looked and found nothing.

properties.name: Foundation crates stay domain-agnostic
properties.statement: The workspace manifest states it as a rule rather than an observation: crates here are INTENTIONALLY domain-neutral, and domain-specific extractors, schemas and servers live in consumer projects that depend on these crates. The pure-math crates go further and take no dependency even on dynograph-core.

properties.name: Cargo feature names are part of the published contract
properties.statement: The `rocksdb` and `fulltext` feature names on dynograph-storage are public API, not internal labels, and must not be renamed or removed without the same care as a breaking change to a function signature. Consumers forward to them BY NAME from their own manifests — reflow2 declares `fulltext = ["dynograph-storage/fulltext"]` and `rocksdb = ["dynograph-storage/rocksdb"]` — so a rename breaks their build instantly, and no published surface, OpenAPI document or public-API semver check would mention it. Recorded because reflow2 declared this reliance and the honest answer at the time was that nothing on this side committed to it.

properties.name: A route behind an unbuilt feature must exist and answer 501
properties.statement: docs/endpoints.md: the routes and the OpenAPI contract ALWAYS exist; a surface whose build feature is off returns 501. So the contract does not change shape with the feature set — a consumer sees the same API and a specific, diagnosable refusal.

properties.name: The full-text index must be a derived, rebuildable view
properties.statement: docs/design-fulltext-primitive.md and the crate doc: Tantivy has its own commit lifecycle and cannot join RocksDB's atomic batch, so the primary store is the source of truth and the index is rebuildable rather than authoritative.

properties.name: The published image should stay near the ~80 MB target
properties.statement: The manifest comment on strip=debuginfo: symbols are kept for readable backtraces, debuginfo is dropped, and the stated aim is bringing a 99.8 MB image down to the canonical ~80 MB target.

properties.name: The MSRV must be pinned in lockstep with the container toolchain
properties.statement: The manifest comment: rust-version is bumped in lockstep with the Dockerfile pin so a local cargo build 'fails loudly on older toolchains rather than via a missing-method error'.

properties.name: One deployment hosts many independent graphs
properties.statement: README: one service hosts many graphs, each with its own schema, so a single deployment is multi-tenant and turnkey.

properties.name: A breaking API change must be caught before release
properties.statement: CI runs cargo-semver-checks against a baseline revision across the workspace. Given consumers pin by git tag and link these crates directly, an unnoticed breaking change lands in their build, not in a registry's version resolution.

properties.name: A caller's raw query string must never reach the query parser
properties.statement: CHANGELOG v0.11.0 states the guarantee is preserved across the ranking change: the raw string is never fed to Tantivy's parser, so `field:value` input cannot inject a filter. A security property held constant while behaviour around it changed.

properties.name: A build without RocksDB must work, and must fail loud rather than fall back
properties.statement: README: RocksDB sits behind a default-on cargo feature; --no-default-features drops it and its ~10-minute C++ compile, leaving the in-memory backend. Such a build 'fails loud if asked to use on-disk storage rather than silently falling back to memory' — the silent-fallback behaviour is explicitly rejected.

properties.name: One generic engine, configured by a schema, becomes a typed graph service
properties.statement: README's headline claim, verbatim in intent: 'one generic engine, configured by a schema, becomes a typed, indexed, searchable graph service — with no code, no migration, and no redeploy.' Each schema declaration is what turns a capability on; the engine must have no hardcoded domain types.

properties.name: Analytics must be scopable to a logical sub-graph
properties.statement: README: because a partitioning field is an indexed PROPERTY rather than a type, the algo/* endpoints can scope analytics to one logical sub-graph inside a shared graph via a where predicate — per-story PageRank being the worked example.

properties.name: Search must not return zero hits for a query that has good partial matches
properties.statement: CHANGELOG v0.11.0, and this is the sharpest recovered requirement in the repo: consumers search BEFORE creating a node and treat an empty result as licence to create, so a false negative manufactured duplicates — 'the index degraded the graph it exists to protect.' The requirement is about what an empty answer MEANS to the caller, not about ranking.

properties.name: A malformed request path must not panic the request
properties.statement: CHANGELOG v0.9.4: a path segment with an RFC-3986-invalid character hit an internal unwrap in the UDS transport and panicked the in-flight request, dropping the connection. Recovered as a requirement because the fix states the general rule, not just the instance.

As of 2026-08-24 the committed design export at docs/design/dynograph-foundation.json had drifted behind the live design: 179 nodes / 270 edges committed, against 186 / 280 in the working store. A strict subset — the committed file held nothing the store lacked.

THE DRIFT IS EXACTLY ONE RELEASE WIDE. Checked: the repo is at v0.13.0 and level with origin/main (0 commits behind, so a pull changes nothing), but the last commit to touch the export is b5a9f74, the v0.12.0 release. v0.13.0 shipped without refreshing it.

The 7 missing nodes are the boundary-types work (req:boundaries-own-their-types, dec:storage-owns-its-hit-type, chg:decouple-fulltext-hit and the questions around them), which matches the v0.12.0 commit 'boundary-type fixes'. That work entered the graph and was never re-exported, so the drift is design work done after the last export, not corruption.

WHY THIS IS WORTH KNOWING: .reflow2/ is deliberately gitignored (the comment on .gitignore:20 says the durable record is an export), and `reflow2 check --export` gates CI on the committed file. A committed export that silently lags means the gate is checking a stale design. Nothing detects the lag on its own, and the release process did not catch it — refreshing the export is not part of the release checklist.

The largest dynograph on-disk store held by any consumer on the development workstation is 152 KB, measured 2026-08-24. It is the only dynograph RocksDB store found there.

Why the number matters: every performance argument about the storage engine, including the RocksDB 11.8.1 LSM-tree work, is unfalsifiable below the scale where an LSM tree has levels to optimize. At 152 KB there is no compaction pressure and the data does not fill a single memtable. No benchmark run against real consumer data would show a difference either way.

This is the number that was missing when the design was found to contain no latency or throughput requirement at all: not only was there no stated budget, there is no workload large enough for one to bind on.

LIMIT: one machine swept. Stores on deployed containers or other hosts were not measured.

Cold build cost of the RocksDB engine bump, measured 2026-08-24 on the maintainer's Linux workstation with `cargo build -p dynograph-storage --example rocksdb_roundtrip --features rocksdb`:

  rocksdb 0.24 / librocksdb-sys 0.17.3+10.4.2 — 414.5 s (6m54s)
  rocksdb 0.25 / librocksdb-sys 0.19.0+11.8.1 — 626.6 s (10m26s)

  +212 s, +51%. Dominated by compiling the C++ engine.

Recorded because the design had NO build-time or performance figure of any kind, which is why the cost side of the upgrade could not be argued at all before this.

SCOPE, because the distinction was got wrong once and corrected: these are COLD builds. Warm incremental builds are NOT affected by the engine version — librocksdb-sys ships a build.rs emitting rerun-if-changed (2 directives, present in 0.17.3 already), so editing Rust code does not rebuild the C++ engine, and the Dockerfile already uses BuildKit cache mounts for /build/target and the cargo registry. Both were true BEFORE this change, so neither is a gain from it. The +51% lands only on fresh CI runs, the published image build, fresh clones, and any Cargo.toml or feature-flag change that invalidates the cache.

COROLLARY WORTH KEEPING: a rebuild of 0.24 forty minutes later took 0.65 s because cargo still held its artifacts — the workstation's target/ directory is 144 GB. Cold-build cost is invisible locally and paid entirely by CI and the image build.

How much of the test suite actually exercises the on-disk backend, measured 2026-08-24 while validating the RocksDB 11.8.1 bump:

  cargo test --workspace (rocksdb feature ON)                952 s
  DYNOGRAPH_TEST_BACKEND=rocksdb cargo test -p dynograph-storage   39 s wall,
      of which 88 tests executing in 0.65 s

The backend-matrix job is the ONLY one that forces the on-disk path — storage tests default to the in-memory backend — and it is the whole of this project's RocksDB coverage. Everything else in that 952 s runs against the in-memory map.

WHY THIS IS WORTH HAVING A NUMBER FOR: a green suite after a storage-engine change is much weaker evidence than it looks. 88 tests in two thirds of a second is what 'the engine still works' rests on. This is thin BY DESIGN and the design says so — RocksDB's cost is compile time, so tests deliberately use the in-memory backend and the rocksdb matrix is a separate CI job — but the consequence is that the code being upgraded is the least-exercised path in the suite. It is also why the C1 batch panic in this project's history reproduced only on RocksDB.

CAVEAT ON COMPLETENESS: recorded while the suite was still running. Three of six debug jobs had finished at the time of writing (default, backend-matrix, fulltext — all rc=0); graph, no-default-features and nodefault+storage-fulltext had not, and the fmt/clippy/release gates had not started. The two timings above are final for their jobs.

Five VERIFIES edges from Verification to Project — ver:clippy, ver:doc-versions, ver:feature-matrix, ver:fmt, ver:release-mode, each pointing at prj:dynograph-foundation — are no longer legal under the current schema, which allows VERIFIES only to Component and Interface. They were dropped on 2026-08-24 to let an import land, because import is all-or-nothing.

WHAT WAS LOST, precisely: each of those five still verifies engine, primitives and surface, but the design has 13 components, so the project-level edge was how 'this gate covers the whole thing' was recorded. That claim is no longer on the record and was NOT re-expressed by fanning the edges out to all 13 components — that would have invented specificity nobody stated.

EXPECT IT TO RECUR: any future import of an export made before the schema tightened will hit the same five. This is a schema-migration artifact, not a one-off. It also means a freshly committed export will carry 275 edges where the last one carried 280, and that difference is this, not data loss in the design work.
